unwrap.title: How Option::unwrap works
unwrap.description: Takes the value out of Some; panics on None.

note.text: fine for Some, a crash for None

slides.caption: unwrap says: I am sure there is a value. If there is not, the program stops.
Some(4): the 4 comes out.
None has no value, so unwrap panics: "called `Option::unwrap()` on a `None` value".
Use unwrap only when None would be a bug. Otherwise prefer unwrap_or, if let, match or ?.

expect.title: How Option::expect works
expect.description: Like unwrap, but the panic message is yours.

slides.caption: expect behaves like unwrap and adds your explanation if it fails.
Some(8080): the value comes out.
None: the program stops with "port must be set", which tells you what went wrong.
Write the message as what you expected: "port must be set", not "error".

unwrap_or.title: How Option::unwrap_or works
unwrap_or.description: The value inside Some, or a default for None.

slides.caption: unwrap_or gives the value if there is one, and the default you pass otherwise.
Some(4): the value, 4.
None: the default, 0.
The default is always computed, even when not needed. For an expensive default, use unwrap_or_else.

unwrap_or_else.title: How Option::unwrap_or_else works
unwrap_or_else.description: The value, or the result of a closure that runs only for None.

note.text: the closure runs only when needed

slides.caption: unwrap_or_else takes a closure instead of a value, so the default is computed lazily.
Some(4): the value. The closure is never called.
None: now the closure runs and its result is used.
Use it when the default is expensive or has side effects, like reading a file.

unwrap_or_default.title: How Option::unwrap_or_default works
unwrap_or_default.description: The value, or the type's default (0, "", empty Vec) for None.

slides.caption: unwrap_or_default uses Default::default() of the type when there is no value.
Some(4): 4.
None for i32: the default i32 is 0. For String it would be "", for Vec an empty Vec.
Short and clear when the type's natural "empty" value is what you want.

map.title: How Option::map works
map.description: Changes the value inside Some; None stays None.

slides.caption: map works on the value if there is one. None skips the closure completely.
Some(4): the closure runs, 4 * 2 = 8, and the result is wrapped again: Some(8).
None: nothing to change, the closure is not called. The result is None.
map lets you work with a possibly missing value without checking for None at every step.

map_or.title: How Option::map_or works
map_or.description: Applies a closure to Some, or returns a default for None.

slides.caption: map_or(default, f) gives f(value) for Some and the default for None.
None: the default, 0.
The result is a plain value, not an Option.

and_then.title: How Option::and_then works
and_then.description: Chains a step that can also fail (return None).

slides.caption: and_then runs the next step only if the previous one gave Some; that step may itself return None.
"5": parse gives Some(5), and 5 > 0, so Some(5).
"-3": parse works, but the check fails: None.
"x": parse already failed, so the check never runs: None.
map would give Some(Some(5)); and_then flattens it. Each step can stop the chain.

ok_or.title: How Option::ok_or works
ok_or.description: Turns Some(v) into Ok(v) and None into Err(your error).

slides.caption: ok_or converts an Option into a Result, so you can use ? on it in a function that returns Result.
Some(4) becomes Ok(4).
None becomes Err("missing"): now the absence has an explanation.
Use ok_or_else when building the error is expensive, like format!.

filter.title: How Option::filter works
filter.description: Keeps Some(v) only if v passes the test.

slides.caption: filter checks the value inside. Failing the test turns Some into None.
4 is even: Some(4) is kept.
3 is odd: the result is None.
None stays None without calling the closure.

take.title: How Option::take works
take.description: Moves the value out and leaves None behind.

title.text: let mut slot = Some(5); let v = slot.take();

slides.caption: take moves the value out of the Option, which is often the only way to take ownership from a struct field.
v gets Some(5).
slot is left as None, so nothing is ever used twice.
Typical in linked lists and state machines: self.head.take().

replace.title: How Option::replace works
replace.description: Puts a new value in and returns the old one.

title.text: let mut slot = Some(1); let old = slot.replace(2);

slides.caption: replace stores the new value and gives back whatever was there before.
The old value comes out: Some(1).
The new value 2 goes in.
If the slot was None, replace returns None and still stores the new value.

is_some.title: How Option::is_some works
is_some.description: true for Some, false for None.

slides.caption: is_some only says whether there is a value; it does not take it out.
Some(4): true.
None: false. is_none() is the opposite.
If you need the value right after checking, use if let Some(v) = opt instead.

zip.title: How Option::zip works
zip.description: Combines two Options into one Option of a pair; None if either is None.

slides.caption: zip gives Some((a, b)) only when both Options have a value.
Both are Some: the result is Some((1, "a")).
One is None, so the pair cannot be made: None.
Handy when two optional values are needed together.

get_or_insert_with.title: How Option::get_or_insert_with works
get_or_insert_with.description: Fills a None with a computed value and returns a reference to the value inside.

slides.caption: get_or_insert_with runs the closure only when the Option is None, stores the result, and lends you the value.
cache is None, so the closure runs and 10 is stored.
The returned &mut lets you change the stored value: 10 + 1 = 11. A second call would not run the closure again.
A simple way to compute something the first time it is needed and reuse it afterwards.

or.title: How Option::or works
or.description: Keeps the first Some; falls back to another Option for None.

slides.caption: or returns self if it has a value, and the other Option otherwise.
Some(4) already has a value: it is kept.
None: the fallback Some(9) is used.
Chain several: user_value.or(config_value).or(Some(default)).

as_ref.title: How Option::as_ref works
as_ref.description: Borrows the value inside: &Option<T> becomes Option<&T>.

slides.caption: map would move the String out of name. as_ref turns it into Option<&String> first, so name stays usable.
as_ref lends the String: Some(&"Ann").
map now gets a &String and returns its length: Some(3). name still owns "Ann".
The classic fix for "use of moved value" errors with Options. as_deref gives Option<&str> directly.
is_none only checks; it does not take anything out.
None: true.
Some(1): false.
In an if, prefer if let Some(x) = opt when you need x afterwards.

map_or_else.title: How Option::map_or_else works
map_or_else.description: Applies one closure to Some and another to None.

slides.caption: map_or_else(default_fn, f): f runs for Some, default_fn for None.
Some("abc"): f gives the length, 3.
None: the default closure runs: "none".len() = 4.
Note the order: the default comes first, the mapping second.

xor.title: How Option::xor works
xor.description: Some if exactly one of the two is Some.

note.text: one or the other, not both

slides.caption: xor keeps a value only when the other side has none.
Only one side has a value: Some(1).
Both have values: None.
Useful for "exactly one of these options must be given" checks.
Nested Options often come from looking something up that may itself be missing.
Some(Some(3)) becomes Some(3).
Some(None) becomes None.
and_then usually avoids creating the nested Option in the first place.

copied.title: How Option::copied works
copied.description: Turns Option<&T> into Option<T> by copying the value.

slides.caption: iter().max() gives Option<&i32>. copied() copies the number out, so the result no longer borrows the array.
The reference &6 inside Some is followed…
…and the value is copied: Some(6).
cloned() does the same for types that are Clone but not Copy, like String.
as_deref borrows the String inside as a &str, so it can be compared with string literals.
Some(String "ann") becomes Some("ann"), a &str.
None stays None, and unwrap_or supplies "anonymous".
Without as_deref, unwrap_or would need a String, and name would be moved.
